doc.title: Nick Brignola interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, July 28, 1997

title: Eclecticism: the late-1960s fusion band and the 'character actor' career
summary: He describes an early electric fusion band, avant-garde and Dixieland work, a day of church, society band and opening for Miles, and taking any gig.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: Exactly. Well I’ve always considered myself that kind of musician. Eclectic is the word? That’s it. I had one of the first electric fusion bands back in the late ‘60s.
I was going to ask about that.

I think I was one of the first guys to run an alto sax through a wa-wa pedal. And I had guys like Dave Holland in my band, and you know guys that just left Miles. I remember one time coming home and listening on the radio, and I was with a bass player, and I said, “Geez that sounds like us.” And it was Weather Report. This was back in the late ‘60s. So I was into that. I played with Dewey Redman and I played some avante garde music. These are experiences that to me I draw upon every time I get up to play. Because every situation is different. I get with a pianist that plays more traditional. I kind of start going in that groove, and kind of hold the fort there, and if I feel I can’t expand that I’m able to jump into another direction because of the experience I’ve had. And all of a

sudden if there’s a piano player who’s harmonically a little bit more advanced, okay, I can go here with this guy, you know. All of a sudden I know what I can do and what I can’t do. So each time is a very individual kind of situation and if you have all of these other experiences to draw from, you never run out of gas. I played with Vic Dickinson and Doc Cheatham, I played, you know Dixieland with these guys, I worked gigs with them. I mean they had their own thing going, their own humor, their own way of doing things, and I worked within that context. So when I come to these jazz parties, some of these same guys, Doc Cheatham, I worked with him twenty years ago, all of a sudden I’m on the bandstand again with him, so it was like old home week. At the same time you sit down and do a duo thing with Roger Kellaway and you need a radar machine to find the harmony sometimes, and we’re doing it at a jazz party. It’s just like — but it works. Because we happen to be playing the theme of a familiar tune, and we departed from it, took it where we wanted and came back, and they always remember the ending, and if you come back with the melody they’re cool. Meanwhile they’ve allowed us to take this space trip. But I think that’s how I’ve been able to survive, is being that character actor, musically. Being able to fit in any musical situation. And I take gigs sometimes that other jazz musicians probably wouldn’t take, but I always find, to me it’s just another experience and I’m going to do the best I can. I remember one time when I had that fusion band, it was on a Saturday, I played a church service, I played alto flute that morning in a church service. And then from twelve to four I played in a society orchestra, with the tux on, playing all the —you know. And then that evening I was the opening act for Miles Davis. So I said, yeah, that’s a pretty good day. To be able to play those three gigs. And I’m saying, you know, who else could do that?
That’s something to pay attention to. That really is.
Yeah. And I took pride in that. But I just, those are the kind of experiences I’ve had, and no gig was too bad for me to take sometimes, you know I always could get something out of it.
And that’s something you don’t learn in school. I mean I’m not sure you can teach that kind of thing, but you learn to deal with it.

No not really. Like if somebody called me for a wedding and I hadn’t played flute for a while, I’d take the flute to the wedding, I’d practice it. It was a chance to play flute for three hours, get paid for it, get my chops up, so you can always make a positive thing out of a negative situation. Instead of saying, “No I’m not going to take that gig, I’m an artist, I don’t play weddings.” Not that I play that many weddings anymore, I’ve been lucky enough to be able to just play jazz really the last few years. But the character actor idea I think has enabled me to survive.
I like that analogy. I may have to use that myself.
I use it all the time.
